entries.meaning: From the time Rāma returned home after his wedding, new auspiciousness, joy and celebration arose every day. Across all fourteen worlds, great mountains of merit caused clouds to rain the water of happiness. Rivers of prosperity, accomplishment and wealth overflowed into Ayodhyā's ocean. Its high-born men and women were like hosts of pure, priceless and beautiful jewels. The city's splendour cannot be described; it seemed the limit of Brahmā's craftsmanship. Seeing the moon of Rāma's face, all the townspeople were happy in every way. The mothers and their companions rejoiced to see the vine of their hopes bear fruit. Hearing and seeing Rāma's beauty, virtues, conduct and nature, the king was delighted. Everyone cherished one wish and prayed to Śiva: while the king still lived, may he give Rāma the office of heir apparent.

Once Daśaratha sat in the royal court with the entire assembly. The king, embodiment of accumulated merit, was thrilled to hear Rāma's fair fame. Every ruler sought his grace, while the guardians of the worlds maintained affection and regard for him. In all three worlds and all three times none was as greatly fortunate as Daśaratha, whose son was Rāma, root of auspiciousness; whatever one might say of his fortune would be little. The king naturally took a mirror in his hand, looked at his face and adjusted his crown. Seeing white hair near his ear, he understood it as old age's counsel: ‘King, give Rāma the heirship; why not take the profit of life and birth?’ Bringing this thought into his heart and finding an auspicious opportunity, the king went joyfully, body thrilled with love, to tell his teacher.

Daśaratha said, ‘Hear me, leader of sages. Rāma has become fully qualified in every way. Servants, ministers, all townspeople, and those who are enemies, friends or neutral toward us—all love Rāma just as I do. Lord, your blessing itself has assumed a body in him. The Brahmins and their families show affection for him, Master, just as they do for you. Those who place the dust of their teacher's feet upon their heads seem to bring every prosperity under their control. None but I has experienced this so fully; by worshipping that sacred dust I have obtained everything. Now one desire remains in my heart: may it be fulfilled, Lord, through your grace.’ Seeing his natural love, the pleased sage asked the king to issue his command: ‘King, your name and fame grant every cherished wish; the fruit follows the desire, jewel among kings, and so will the wish in your heart.’

Knowing his teacher was pleased in every way, Daśaratha spoke softly with a smile: ‘Lord, let Rāma be made heir apparent; graciously give the word and have the assembly prepared. While I remain alive, let this celebration occur so that everyone may obtain the reward of their eyes. By your grace and Śiva's, every undertaking has been completed; this alone remains as the longing in my heart. Then I shall have no concern whether this body stays or goes, and there will be no regret afterward.’ Hearing the king's auspicious words, which were roots of joy and celebration, the sage was pleased: ‘Hear, king: those who turn away from him repent, and the burning of existence cannot cease without worshipping him. That very Master has become your son—holy Rāma, follower of love. Make no delay; prepare the whole occasion swiftly. The auspicious day and hour are precisely when Rāma becomes heir apparent.’

The delighted king returned to the palace and summoned servants, ministers and Sumantra. They bowed and offered the victory greeting, and the king told them the auspicious news. ‘If the opinion of all five accords with it, joyfully arrange Rāma's anointing.’ Hearing the beloved words, the delighted minister seemed like a cherished tree receiving water. The ministers joined their hands and prayed, ‘May you live for crores of years, lord of the world. You have considered an undertaking good for the world's welfare; hasten it, Lord, and allow no delay.’ Hearing the minister's eloquent words, the king's joy grew like a dwarfed tree receiving a fine branch. He said, ‘Swiftly carry out, for Rāma's royal anointing, each command given by the king of sages.’

The lord of sages joyfully said in a gentle voice, ‘Bring water from every holy river, and the many named herbs, roots, flowers, fruits and leaves that are auspicious. Bring fly-whisks, hides and many kinds of garments; hair-cloths, silks and countless textiles; hosts of jewels and every auspicious object in the world suitable for a king's anointing.’ After stating every rite known in the Vedas, he ordered the city adorned with varied canopies: ‘Plant fruit-laden mangoes, areca palms and plantains all around the city's streets. Fashion lovely, beautiful jewelled designs in the courtyards and have the markets decorated quickly. Worship Gaṇeśa, the teacher and the family deities, and serve the Brahmins in every way. Adorn banners, pennants, arches and pitchers, horses, chariots and elephants.’ Placing the eminent sage's words upon their heads, everyone went to their respective tasks.

Whatever order the lord of sages gave to each person, that task seemed completed at once. The king worshipped Brahmins, holy people and gods and performed auspicious acts for Rāma. On hearing the lovely news of Rāma's anointing, congratulations resounded densely through Ayodhyā. Auspicious signs appeared in Rāma's and Sītā's bodies; their lovely limbs quivered propitiously. Thrilled with love, they told one another that these omens foretold Bharata's arrival. Many days had passed; at last the signs promised a meeting with their beloved. ‘Who in the world is as dear as Bharata? These omens can have no other fruit.’ Rāma worried for his brother day and night as a tortoise's heart remains with its eggs. At that moment, hearing this supreme good news, the women's quarters smiled, looking like the ocean's sportive waves swelling at the sight of the waxing moon.

Those who first brought the news received abundant ornaments and garments. Their bodies thrilled with love, their minds full of affection, and everyone began adorning auspicious pitchers. Sumitrā fashioned beautiful courtyard designs, filling the city with many exquisite jewelled patterns. Immersed in joy, Rāma's mother summoned Brahmins and gave many gifts. She worshipped the village goddesses, gods and serpent deities and promised additional offerings: ‘By whatever means Rāma's welfare may be secured, graciously grant that boon.’ Women with cuckoo-like voices, moon-like faces and fawn-like eyes sang auspicious songs. Hearing of Rāma's royal anointing, men and women rejoiced in their hearts and began every propitious preparation, judging the circumstances wholly favourable.

Daśaratha then summoned Vasiṣṭha and sent him to Rāma's home to give instruction. Hearing of his teacher's arrival, Rāma came to the door and bowed his head at his feet. Respectfully offering water of welcome, he brought Vasiṣṭha inside, worshipped him in the sixteen ways and honoured him. Rāma again clasped his feet with Sītā, joined lotus-like hands and said, ‘A master's arrival at a servant's house is the root of blessing and the destruction of misfortune. Even so, proper custom is to call the servant lovingly and send him on the task, Lord. Abandoning lordly distance, Master, you have shown affection; today this home has become holy. Whatever your command, I shall perform it, Lord; a servant gains fulfilment through serving the master.’ Hearing the words steeped in love, the sage praised Rāma: ‘How could you not speak thus, ornament of the swan-like solar line?’

Describing Rāma's virtues, conduct and nature, the sage-king spoke with love and a thrilled body: ‘The king has prepared the entire anointing assembly and wishes to give you the heirship. Rāma, observe every discipline today, so that Fate may successfully complete the undertaking.’ Giving his instruction, Vasiṣṭha went to the king. Rāma felt inward wonder: ‘All the brothers were born together; eating, sleeping and childhood play were shared. Ear-piercing, investiture and marriage all occurred together and were celebrations for all. In this spotless lineage, one thing is unfitting: to leave the brothers aside and anoint only the eldest.’ Rāma's beautiful, loving regret removes crookedness from devotees' minds. At that moment Lakṣmaṇa arrived, immersed in love and joy. Rāma, moon to the night-lotuses of Raghu's line, honoured him with affectionate words.
